mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-01.title: Bounding square
mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-01.body:
A circle of area $\pi$ has radius $1$. Let its center be $(p,q)$. The disk lies inside the square $[p-1,p+1]\times[q-1,q+1]$, so a unit block $[a,a+1]\times[b,b+1]$ can contain a point of the disk (in its interior) only if $a<p+1$ and $a+1>p-1$, i.e. $a\in(p-2,p+1)$, and likewise $b\in(q-2,q+1)$.

An open interval of length $3$ contains at most $3$ integers. So there are at most $3$ possible values of $a$ and at most $3$ possible values of $b$, hence at most $3\cdot3=9$ unit blocks can be covered (partly) by the circle. ∎

mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-02.title: Sweep line
mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-02.body:
Choose a direction not parallel to any of the lines through two of the points, and rotate the plane so that this direction is the $x$-axis; then all $2016$ points have distinct $x$-coordinates. Sort the points by $x$-coordinate and split them into $504$ groups $G_1,\dots,G_{504}$ of four consecutive points.

In each group $G_i$ we can choose a *simple* (non-self-intersecting) quadrilateral on its four points: if the four points are in convex position, take the convex hull; otherwise one point lies inside the triangle formed by the other three (no three points are collinear), and joining it to two vertices of the triangle yields a simple (non-convex) quadrilateral.

The quadrilateral $Q_i$ lies in the convex hull of $G_i$, hence in the vertical strip between the smallest and the largest $x$-coordinate of $G_i$. For $i<j$ every point of $G_i$ has smaller $x$ than every point of $G_j$, so these strips are disjoint. Hence $Q_i$ and $Q_j$ share no vertex, no edge and no point, so the $504$ quadrilaterals are pairwise disjoint. ∎

mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-03.title: Work modulo 11
mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-03.body:
We would need $x^5+y^5+z^5+t^5=2016^3$. For any integer $n$: if $11\mid n$ then $n^5\equiv0\pmod{11}$; otherwise $(n^5)^2=n^{10}\equiv1\pmod{11}$ by Fermat's little theorem, so $n^5\equiv\pm1\pmod{11}$. Hence each fifth power is congruent to $0$, $1$ or $-1$, and the sum of four of them is congruent to one of $-4,-3,\dots,3,4$, i.e. to one of the residues $0,1,2,3,4,7,8,9,10$ modulo $11$.

But $2016=11\cdot183+3$, so $2016^3\equiv3^3=27\equiv5\pmod{11}$, and $5$ is not among those residues. So no such integers exist. ∎

mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-04.title: Symmetric functions, then three cases
mmaths-2016-tiebreaker-04.body:
Let $q=ab+bc+ca$ and $r=abc$ (recall $a+b+c=3$). Since $a^2(b-c)^2=(ab-ac)^2$, summing gives $\sum a^2(b-c)^2=2\sum a^2b^2-2abc(a+b+c)=2(q^2-6r)-6r=2q^2-18r$. So the inequality is equivalent to
$$F:=4q^2-45r+9r^2\ge0.$$

**Case 1: $r\le0$.** Then $F\ge4q^2\ge0$. Equality needs $r=0$ and $q=0$: if $c=0$ then $a+b=3$ and $q=ab=0$, giving $(3,0,0)$ and its permutations.

**Case 2: $r>0$ and two variables negative.** Say $a>0>b,c$; write $b=-\beta$, $c=-\gamma$, $S=\beta+\gamma>0$, $P=\beta\gamma\le S^2/4$. Then $a=3+S$, $q=P-aS$, $r=aP$. Because $aS-P\ge aS-S^2/4\ge S\left(3+\frac{3S}{4}\right)$, we get $4q^2\ge36S^2\left(1+\frac S4\right)^2=36S^2+18S^3+\frac94S^4$, while $45r=45aP\le\frac{45}{4}(3+S)S^2=\frac{135}{4}S^2+\frac{45}{4}S^3$. Hence $4q^2-45r\ge\frac94S^2+\frac{27}{4}S^3+\frac94S^4>0$, so $F>0$.

**Case 3: $a,b,c>0$.** Let $c$ be the largest, so $1\le c<3$. Put $t=\frac{a+b}{2}=\frac{3-c}{2}$ and $m=ab\le t^2$. Then $q=m+2tc$, $r=cm$ and
$$F(m)=4(m+2tc)^2-45cm+9c^2m^2=(4+9c^2)m^2+(16t-45)c\,m+16t^2c^2,$$
a convex quadratic in $m$.

*Value at $m=t^2$ (i.e. $a=b=t$, $c=3-2t$):* $q=t^2+2t(3-2t)=6t-3t^2$ and $r=t^2(3-2t)$, and expanding gives $F(t^2)=9t^2(1-t)^2(1-2t)^2\ge0$, which is $0$ only for $t=1$ (point $(1,1,1)$) or $t=\frac12$ (point $(\frac12,\frac12,2)$).

*Slope at $m=t^2$:* $F'(t^2)=2(4+9c^2)t^2+(16t-45)c=\frac12(3-c)^2(4+9c^2)-c(21+8c)=\frac12g(c)$, where $g(c)=9c^4-54c^3+69c^2-66c+36=9c^2(3-c)^2-12c^2-66c+36$. For $1\le c\le2$ we have $c(3-c)\le2c$, so $g(c)\le36c^2-12c^2-66c+36=6(4c-3)(c-2)\le0$, with strict inequality for $c<2$, and $g(2)=-108<0$. For $2\le c\le3$ we have $c(3-c)\le2$, so $g(c)\le36-48-132+36<0$. Hence $F'(t^2)<0$.

Since $F$ is convex and $m-t^2\le0$: $F(m)\ge F(t^2)+F'(t^2)(m-t^2)\ge F(t^2)\ge0$. Equality forces $m=t^2$, i.e. $a=b$, and $F(t^2)=0$.

**Conclusion.** The inequality holds for all real $a,b,c$ with $a+b+c=3$, with equality exactly when $(a,b,c)$ is a permutation of $(1,1,1)$, $\left(\frac12,\frac12,2\right)$ or $(3,0,0)$. ∎
